steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
Alternating direction method of multipliers
- ADMM: variant of augmented Lagrangian scheme, partial updates for dual variables
- typical problem: \min_x f(x) + g(Mx).
- equivalent constrained problem: \min_{x,y} f(x) + g(y), \quad \text{subject to}\quad Mx = y.
- why it helps
  - seems trivial, but now constrained optimization methods apply (esp. augmented Lagrangian)
  - objective separable in x and y
- updates
  - dual update needs proximity function in x and y at same time
  - ADMM: approx. solve x with y fixed, then y with x fixed
  - no iterating to convergence (unlike Jacobi method); go straight to dual update, repeat
  - not equal to exact minimization, still converges to correct solution under some assumptions
  - doesn't (approx.) minimize augmented Lagrangian -> distinct from ordinary ALM
- relations: application of Douglas-Rachford splitting; D-R is instance of Proximal point algorithm; details in ref.
- software
  - Basis pursuit and variants: YALL1 (2009), SpaRSA (2009), SALSA (2009)
  - more general problems, some multi-core: SNAPVX (2015), parADMM (2016)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) is a variant of the augmented Lagrangian scheme. It uses partial updates for the dual variables. The method is often used to solve problems like

\min_x f(x) + g(Mx).

This is the same as the constrained problem

\min_{x,y} f(x) + g(y), \quad \text{subject to}\quad Mx = y.

This change may look trivial, but now the problem can be attacked with methods of constrained optimization (in particular the augmented Lagrangian method), and the objective function is separable in x and y.

- dual update needs proximity function in x and y together
- ADMM approx.: x with y fixed, then y with x fixed; no iterating to convergence (unlike Jacobi method), go straight to dual update, repeat
- not same as exact minimization but converges to correct solution under some assumptions
- doesn't minimize augmented Lagrangian -> distinct from ordinary ALM
- application of Douglas-Rachford splitting; D-R instance of Proximal point algorithm; details in ref.
- software: YALL1 (2009), SpaRSA (2009), SALSA (2009) for Basis pursuit and variants; SNAPVX (2015), parADMM (2016) for more general problems, some multi-core

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) is a variant of the augmented Lagrangian scheme. It uses partial updates for the dual variables. The method is often used to solve problems like

\min_x f(x) + g(Mx).

This is the same as the constrained problem

\min_{x,y} f(x) + g(y), \quad \text{subject to}\quad Mx = y.

This change may look trivial, but now the problem can be attacked with methods of constrained optimization (in particular the augmented Lagrangian method), and the objective function is separable in x and y.
The dual update needs solving a proximity function in x and y at the same time. The ADMM technique lets this problem be solved approximately, by first solving for x with y fixed and after that solving for y with x fixed. The ADMM algorithm does not iterate this process until convergence (like the Jacobi method does), instead it goes directly to updating the dual variable and then it repeats the process. This is not the same as the exact minimization, but under some assumptions the method still converges to the correct solution. The algorithm does not minimize or approximately minimize the augmented Lagrangian, so it is distinct from the ordinary augmented Lagrangian method.

The ADMM can be seen as an application of the Douglas-Rachford splitting algorithm, and the Douglas-Rachford algorithm in turn is an instance of the Proximal point algorithm; details can be found in the literature. Several modern software packages solve Basis pursuit and variants and use the ADMM, including YALL1 (2009), SpaRSA (2009) and SALSA (2009). There are also packages that use the ADMM for more general problems, and some of these can exploit multiple computing cores (e.g., SNAPVX (2015), parADMM (2016)).

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) is a variant of the augmented Lagrangian scheme that uses partial updates for the dual variables. This method is often applied to solve problems such as

\min_x f(x) + g(Mx).

This is equivalent to the constrained problem

\min_{x,y} f(x) + g(y), \quad \text{subject to}\quad Mx = y.

Though this change may seem trivial, the problem can now be attacked using methods of constrained optimization (in particular, the augmented Lagrangian method), and the objective function is separable in x and y. The dual update requires solving a proximity function in x and y at the same time; the ADMM technique allows this problem to be solved approximately by first solving for x with y fixed and then solving for y with x fixed. Instead of iterating this process until convergence (like the Jacobi method), the ADMM algorithm proceeds directly to updating the dual variable and then repeats the process. This is not equivalent to the exact minimization, but the method still converges to the correct solution under some assumptions. Because it does not minimize or approximately minimize the augmented Lagrangian, the algorithm is distinct from the ordinary augmented Lagrangian method.

The ADMM can be viewed as an application of the Douglas-Rachford splitting algorithm, and the Douglas-Rachford algorithm is in turn an instance of the Proximal point algorithm; details can be found in ref.[1] Several modern software packages, including YALL1[2] (2009), SpaRSA[3] (2009) and SALSA[4] (2009), solve Basis pursuit and variants and use the ADMM. Other packages use the ADMM to solve more general problems, and some of them can exploit multiple computing cores (e.g., SNAPVX[5] (2015), parADMM[6] (2016)).

References:
[1] Eckstein, Jonathan. (April 1992). On the Douglas—Rachford splitting method and the proximal point algorithm for maximal monotone operators. Mathematical Programming. doi:10.1007/BF01581204
[2] YALL1: Your ALgorithms for L1. yall1.blogs.rice.edu. http://yall1.blogs.rice.edu/
[3] SpaRSA. www.lx.it.pt. https://www.lx.it.pt/~mtf/SpaRSA/
